subject: Tertullian (Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus)

text_used.text: Every quotation of Tertullian below is checked word for word against the Ante-Nicene Fathers, vols. 3 and 4 (American edition, 1885), downloaded whole as plain text from CCEL (marked Public Domain), and against the CCEL chapter page given as its url. Translators: S. Thelwall (most works), Peter Holmes (Prescription, Against Marcion, On the Soul, Flesh of Christ, Resurrection, Praxeas), Alexander Roberts (Against the Valentinians). Jerome is checked against NPNF 2nd series vols. 3 and 6; Vincent of Lerins against NPNF 2nd series vol. 11; Eusebius against NPNF 2nd series vol. 1. 'exact' is the translation as printed, with footnote numbers taken out. 'vol' names the raw volume file and 'page' the chapter file in sources/people/tertullian/ that the checker script matches it against (design/saints-hub/tools/check-tertullian.mjs: 120 checks, 0 failures on 2026-09-24; case-insensitive, whitespace collapsed, footnote marks removed). The chapter-page files were fetched with CCEL's footnotes stripped out. research/people/tertullian.quotes.json holds 51 entries in the verify-quotes.mjs format (display = exact, file = the chapter page), all found; the war line is left out of it because the print has 'un- belted' across a line break. No Tertullian quotation below needs a capitals change for God: the ANF already prints He/His for God where they occur.
text_used.source: CCEL plain-text volumes anf03.txt, anf04.txt, npnf201.txt, npnf203.txt, npnf206.txt, npnf211.txt
text_used.note: New Advent's copies (Kevin Knight's lightly revised text) match these lines except where noted. ONE CORRUPTION IN BOTH ONLINE COPIES: On Idolatry, chapter 19 reads 'unbe**d every soldier' on CCEL and New Advent alike. The printed Edinburgh edition (Ante-Nicene Christian Library vol. 11, 1869, same Thelwall translation) reads 'un- belted every soldier' (archive.org scan AnteNiceneChristianLibraryV11, djvu text), and the Latin is 'omnem postea militem dominus in Petro exarmando discinxit' (tertullian.org Latin text). So the site's 'unbelted' is right; the free links show a garbled word.

name.text: Latin name Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus. He signs one of his own books 'Septimius Tertullianus'.
name.source: Encyclopedia of Religion (E. Glenn Hinson, 1987), 'Tertullian', via Encyclopedia.com: 'TERTULLIAN (160?-225?), Quintus Septimius Florens'; On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 17 (last lines): 'may peace and grace from our Lord Jesus Christ redound: as likewise to Septimius Tertullianus, whose this tractate is.'
name.note: The New Catholic Encyclopedia prints 'Septimus' (a typo for Septimius).

born.text: About 160, probably at Carthage in Roman Africa, today near Tunis in Tunisia. Some put it a few years earlier (Britannica: 155/160).
born.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), 'Tertullian': 'b. probably about 160 at Carthage'; New Catholic Encyclopedia (W. Le Saint), via Encyclopedia.com: 'b. probably at Carthage, c. 160; d. after 220'; Jerome, Illustrious Men 53: 'from the city of Carthage in the province of Africa'; Britannica (search-result text only): 'born c. 155/160, Carthage'
born.note: The site's 'c. 155' is at the early end. Britannica's own page returned 403 to every fetch; its dates were read only in a search result. McGiffert's note to Eusebius 2.2 (NPNF2-1) records that Lipsius and Noldechen put the birth about 150. Safe wording: 'Born about 160 (some say 155), at Carthage'. 'Today near Tunis' is ordinary geography: ancient Carthage lies in the suburbs of Tunis; the Encyclopedia of Religion and the fathers research say 'Roman Africa (modern Tunisia)'.
born.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Britannica checked directly on 2026-09-25: "born c. 155/160, Carthage". "Some say 155" now stands on a source that was opened.

family.text: His father was a centurion. Jerome says 'the son of a proconsul or Centurion'. The Catholic Encyclopedia reads it as a centurion in the proconsul's service. He was married, and wrote two books to his wife.
family.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53 (NPNF2-3, tr. E. C. Richardson); Catholic Encyclopedia (1912): 'the son of a centurion in the proconsular service'; New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'He was certainly married'; To His Wife, Books 1 and 2
family.note: Vincent's footnote, quoting Kaye's version of Jerome, has 'the son of a proconsular centurion'. Richardson's 'proconsul or Centurion' is a clumsy rendering of the Latin 'centurionis proconsularis'.

grew_up.text: A pagan until middle life. He was well educated, especially in rhetoric and law. He laughed at the Christian faith himself before he believed it.
grew_up.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912): 'A pagan until middle life, he had shared the pagan prejudices against Christianity, and had indulged like others in shameful pleasures.' New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'received an excellent education, chiefly in rhetoric and jurisprudence'. Apology, chapter 18: 'Once these things were with us, too, the theme of ridicule.'
grew_up.note: Whether he practised law at Rome is disputed (see misquoted, 'a Roman lawyer').

converted.text: Became a Christian by 197, perhaps about 195.
converted.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912): 'His conversion was not later than the year 197, and may have been earlier.' New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'Converted to Christianity (c. 195)'. Encyclopedia of Religion: 'around 193 to 195'.

died.text: Date, place and cause unknown. After 220. Jerome says he was said to have lived to a very great age.
died.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53: 'He is said to have lived to a decrepit old age'. New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'd. after 220'. Encyclopedia of Religion: 'The exact date of his death is unknown.' Britannica (search text only): 'died after 220, Carthage'.
died.note: Only Britannica names Carthage as the place of death, and I could not open its page. Print 'Where and when he died is not known' unless Britannica is checked.
died.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Britannica opened on 2026-09-25 (HTTP 200): "born c. 155/160, Carthage—died after 220, Carthage" (saved as sources/people/tertullian/britannica-tertullian.txt). No early source names the place. The page now says so, and Britannica is in the sources list, which also carries "Some say 155".

buried.text: Unknown. No source records a grave.
buried.source: No ancient or modern source read here mentions his burial.

also_called.text: No church gives him a title. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls him an 'ecclesiastical writer'. The Russian Orthodox site azbyka.ru calls him an 'outstanding church writer'.
also_called.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), first line: 'Ecclesiastical writer in the second and third centuries'; azbyka.ru, 'Тертуллиан': 'признается выдающимся церковным писателем' (he is recognised as an outstanding church writer)
also_called.note: The fathers research lists 'Tertullian of Carthage' as another name. It is a common descriptive form, not a title; no source was needed or found.

status.text: Not counted a saint by any church. He joined the New Prophecy (Montanism) and broke with the Church.
status.note: CAUTION ON THE WORDS 'Church Father': the README's status line is 'Church Father. Not counted a saint.' Two sources refuse him that title. New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'he cannot be recommended without reserve to Christian readers or honored with a place among the fathers of the church.' azbyka.ru: 'Из-за отпадения от Церкви он не почитается отцом Церкви' (Because he fell away from the Church he is not honoured as a Father of the Church). Many others do call him one loosely (the Ante-Nicene Fathers series prints him; the Catholic Encyclopedia calls him 'the first of Latin theological writers'). Suggested honest line: 'Early Church writer. Not counted a saint.' Or keep 'Church Father' with a note that Catholic and Orthodox writers withhold the title. The owner should choose.

patron_of.text: None. No patronage is recorded, which fits: he is not a saint.
patron_of.source: No source read here gives one. Wikidata (people-audit.json) lists 0 patron-of items.

in_art.text: No portrait from his lifetime or the ancient Church is known. From the 1580s printers made up likenesses: André Thevet's turbaned, bearded writer with a scroll (1584), a woodcut in Pamelius's edition of his works (Paris, 1584), and later French and Dutch engravings.
in_art.source: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (file pages for Tertullian2.png, Tertvlliani Effigies bub gb rB A8s1pn8EC 0214.jpg, Tertullien, PA02213.jpg, TERTVLLIAN AF CART PRESB.jpg); British Museum description of 1879,1213.146: 'a turbaned, bearded man seen half-length, turned to the right, holding a parchment scroll; illustration to Thevet's Les vrais pourtraits'
in_art.note: 'No ancient likeness is known' rests on absence: the fathers research says so and nothing older than 1584 turns up on Commons except manuscripts of his text. No Eastern icon of him exists that I could find, which fits his status. Call the portraits 'imagined'.
in_art.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "From 1584" rests only on what Commons holds (an absence). The page now says "Later engravers imagined him: as a writer in a turban in 1584, or as a bald old man with a long beard." Both pictures checked by eye.

wrote.text: Thirty-one treatises survive, all in Latin. At least twelve more are lost, some of them written in Greek. His longest work is Against Marcion, in five books.
wrote.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'Thirty-one authentic treatises of Tertullian are extant. Five others attributed to him are spurious, and there are at least twelve that have been lost, including three of four written originally in Greek.' Encyclopedia of Religion: 'Tertullian's writings, thirty-one of which are extant'. Catholic Encyclopedia: 'his largest extant work, five books against Marcion'; 'He knew Greek as well as Latin, and wrote works in Greek which have not come down to us.'

pronounced.source: Dictionary.com (Random House Unabridged): 'ter-tuhl-ee-uhn, -tuhl-yuhn', IPA tərˈtʌl i ən, -ˈtʌl jən; Collins English Dictionary (British, on the same page): /tɜːˈtʌlɪən/
pronounced.note: Merriam-Webster, Collins's own site and Britannica returned 403 (bot check). The Collins entry is quoted on Dictionary.com's page with its copyright line. Stress on the second syllable in both.
pronounced.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: order swapped: Dictionary.com gives [ter-tuhl-ee-uhn] first and -tuhl-yuhn second.

roles.name: Convert
roles.text: Became a Christian by 197, perhaps about 195.
roles.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page had "About 195, at Carthage". No source says where he was converted (the NCE puts his law practice at Rome). Now "About 195, as a grown man" (Catholic Encyclopedia: "A pagan until middle life").

roles.name: Defender
roles.text: Wrote the Apology in 197, addressed to the Roman governors, to show that Christians were persecuted unjustly.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'The year 197 saw the publication of ... the Ad nationes and the Apologeticus'; New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'It was addressed to the provincial governors of the Roman Empire'; Apology, chapter 1: 'Rulers of the Roman Empire'

roles.name: Theologian
roles.line: The first to write theology in Latin
roles.text: The first of the Latin theological writers. The first known writer to call God 'Trinity' (trinitas) in Latin.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'He is the first of Latin theological writers.' New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'As far as is known, the first use of the Latin word trinitas with reference to God is found in Tertullian's Adversus Praxean and De pudicitia. He was the first to use the term persona in a Trinitarian and Christological context'
roles.note: Say 'in Latin'. Theophilus of Antioch used the Greek word earlier (see misquoted).

roles.name: Montanist
roles.text: Joined the New Prophecy after 206, and broke with the Church about 211 to 213.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'It was after the year 206 that he joined the Montanist sect, and he seems to have definitively separated from the Church about 211 (Harnack) or 213 (Monceaux).' His own words, Against Praxeas 1: 'We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete.'
roles.note: The fathers research says 'about 207'; the site says 'Later in life he joined the New Prophecy'. Both fit 'after 206'.

roles.name: Founder
roles.text: Later he left the Montanists too and led a group of his own, the Tertullianists. Their last members rejoined the Church in Augustine's time.
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'he separated from the Montanists and founded a sect of his own. The remnant of the Tertullianists was reconciled to the Church by St. Augustine.' Augustine, On Heresies 86 (Latin): 'Paucissimi enim qui remanserant, in Catholicam transierunt, suamque basilicam ... Catholicae tradiderunt.'
roles.note: The Encyclopedia of Religion agrees (he 'formed a sect of his own called Tertullianists'). Some modern scholars doubt that he founded it; the sources above do not, so state it as they do.

summary.text: None. No church keeps a feast for him. He is not in the Catholic calendar or the Roman Martyrology, not in the Orthodox calendar, and not in the Anglican, Episcopal or Lutheran calendars.
summary.source: Checked against each church's own list (below).
summary.note: Leave the feasts section out, or show one plain line: 'No church keeps a feast day for him.'

catholic.text: No feast. The 1916 Roman Martyrology has no entry for him. It does have a different St Tertullian, a bishop of Bologna, on 27 April.
catholic.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 27 April: 'At Bologna, St. Tertullian, bishop and confessor.' Index: 'Tertullian, St., B., C..Apr. 27'. The General Roman Calendar has no Tertullian.
catholic.note: Checked in the full OCR text saved for Martin (sources/people/martin-of-tours/martyrology-1916.txt, lines 4258 and 22964). The 2004 Martyrology was not checked.

orthodox.text: No feast. The Russian Orthodox site azbyka.ru says he is not honoured as a Father of the Church, because he fell away into Montanism.
orthodox.source: azbyka.ru, 'Тертуллиан': 'Отпал от Церкви в монтанизм.' (He fell away from the Church into Montanism.) 'Из-за отпадения от Церкви он не почитается отцом Церкви, но признается выдающимся церковным писателем' (Because of his falling away he is not honoured as a Father of the Church, but is recognised as an outstanding church writer). OrthodoxWiki, 'Tertullian': 'he ended his life leading his own sect after have joining the Montanist movement.'
orthodox.note: OCA's site search returned no saint of that name; its 31 August page mentions him only as the writer whose works helped convert St Cyprian. OrthodoxWiki is a wiki, not a church body.

anglican.text: No commemoration. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar keeps Perpetua (7 March) and Cyprian (15 September) of Carthage, but not Tertullian.
anglican.note: Searched the fetched page for 'Tertull': no match. Control: 'Perpetua' and 'Cyprian' found.

episcopal.text: No commemoration in Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022. He is named once, in the entry for Thecla, as a writer.
episcopal.source: The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (PDF): 'According to Tertullian (writing around the year 200), early Christian women appealed to Thecla's example to defend women's freedom to teach and to baptize.'
episcopal.note: Full text extracted with pdftotext; one match only.

lutheran.text: No commemoration by the Missouri Synod (Lutheran Service Book) or the ELCA (Evangelical Lutheran Worship).
lutheran.source: LCMS, 'Commemorations' (lists Perpetua and Felicitas 7 March, Cyprian 16 September; no Tertullian); CPH, 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations'; Evangelical Lutheran Worship church-year list (2006, archived PDF)
lutheran.note: Controls found in each list (Perpetua, Cyprian).

why.text: He left the Church for the New Prophecy, so no church honours him as a saint.

numbers.text: Thirty-one authentic treatises survive; at least twelve are lost.
numbers.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia ('Thirty-one authentic treatises of Tertullian are extant ... at least twelve that have been lost'); Encyclopedia of Religion ('thirty-one of which are extant')

lines: Against a man who cut up the Gospels
numbers.text: Against Marcion, in five books, is his largest surviving work.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('his largest extant work, five books against Marcion'); Encyclopedia of Religion ('the longest of his writings')
numbers.note: 'Cut up the Gospels' rests on his own 'he who has gnawed the Gospels to pieces' (Against Marcion 1.1).

numbers.text: 'there are almost a thousand neologisms in Tertullian'
numbers.note: Print 'almost 1,000'. Trinitas is the famous one.

numbers.text: 'He quoted from more than 100 different authors'
numbers.note: Useful against the idea that he despised learning.

numbers.text: 'The party that he founded continued in existence for some 200 years, the last remnant being reconciled to the Church by St. Augustine (c. 400).'
numbers.source: New Catholic Encyclopedia; Augustine, On Heresies 86

numbers.text: Jerome: he wrote 'six books On ecstasy, and a seventh which he wrote Against Apollonius', all lost.
numbers.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53 and 40; Catholic Encyclopedia ('Of the lost works of Tertullian the most important was the defence of the Montanist manner of prophesying, De ecstasi, in six books, with a seventh book against Apollonius.')
numbers.note: Optional; the first four are stronger.

traits.title: impatient, and said so
traits.text: He wrote a whole book on patience. In the first chapter he admits he has none.
traits.exact: So I, most miserable, ever sick with the heats of impatience, must of necessity sigh after, and invoke, and persistently plead for, that health of patience which I possess not
traits.note: The New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'It is true that he was impatient and irritable, but it is equally true that he was honest enough to admit this in the introduction to his beautiful treatise De patientia.'

traits.title: a mocking wit
traits.text: He argued that some ideas deserve laughter, not a serious reply. He called Marcion worse than a Pontic mouse.
traits.exact: Vain and silly topics are met with especial fitness by laughter. Even the truth may indulge in ridicule, because it is jubilant; it may play with its enemies, because it is fearless.
traits.exact2: What Pontic mouse ever had such gnawing powers as he who has gnawed the Gospels to pieces?
traits.cite: Against the Valentinians, chapter 6; Against Marcion, Book 1, chapter 1
traits.note: CCEL prints 'especial fitness'; New Advent and the fathers research have 'special fitness'. Use 'especial'. He adds in the same place: 'Only we must take care that its laughter be not unseemly'. Against the Valentinians is Alexander Roberts's translation.

traits.title: never ashamed to change his mind
traits.text: When critics threw his old views back at him, he was glad to have changed. He was proud to stand with the few.
traits.exact: I blush not at an error which I have ceased to hold, because I am delighted at having ceased to hold it, because I recognise myself to be better and more modest. No one blushes at his own improvement.
traits.exact2: As if it were not easier to err with the majority, when it is in the company of the few that truth is loved!
traits.note: Written in his Montanist years, against a bishop's edict pardoning adultery. The 'error' he renounces is his own earlier, milder view.
traits.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: On Modesty 1 does not say critics threw his views back. He writes that he will add a count against the Psychics "in order that they may the more cast this in my teeth for a mark of fickleness": he expects the charge. The page now says "He knew his critics would call him fickle for leaving his old, milder views."

traits.title: tender at home
traits.text: The man who wrote so harshly also wrote one of the warmest early pictures of Christian marriage, in a book to his own wife.
traits.exact: Together they pray, together prostrate themselves, together perform their fasts; mutually teaching, mutually exhorting, mutually sustaining.
traits.note: Earlier in the chapter, exact: 'Whence are we to find (words) enough fully to tell the happiness of that marriage which the Church cements, and the oblation confirms, and the benediction signs and seals; (which) angels carry back the news of (to heaven), (which) the Father holds for ratified?' 'One of the warmest pictures' is our judgement; the New Catholic Encyclopedia calls it 'The beautiful treatise addressed to his wife'.

others_on_him.who: St Cyprian of Carthage, as Jerome heard it from Cyprian's old secretary
others_on_him.exact: He said that he himself had seen how Cyprian was accustomed never to pass a day without reading Tertullian, and that he frequently said to him, "Give me the master," meaning by this, Tertullian.
others_on_him.cite: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 53
others_on_him.note: Jerome met 'a certain Paul an old man of Concordia' who had been Cyprian's secretary as a very young man. Jerome also writes (Letter 84, section 2): 'The blessed Cyprian takes Tertullian for his master, as his writings prove; yet ... he does not join him in following Montanus and Maximilla.' CCEL's chapter id for chapter 53 is npnf203.v.iii.lv.

others_on_him.exact: Every word almost was a sentence; every sentence a victory.
others_on_him.exact_more: Yet this man also, notwithstanding all that I have mentioned, this Tertullian, I say, too little tenacious of Catholic doctrine, that is, of the universal and ancient faith, more eloquent by far than faithful, changed his belief
others_on_him.note: Same chapter: 'For as Origen holds by far the first place among the Greeks, so does Tertullian among the Latins.' And he calls him 'a great trial in the Church'. Vincent wrote about 434 (the Commonitory's own dating, three years after Ephesus); he did not know Tertullian. The date is from the NPNF introduction, not re-read here.

others_on_him.exact: In the case of Tertullian we praise his great talent, but we condemn his heresy.
others_on_him.cite: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 3, section 27
others_on_him.note: Also Jerome, Letter 70, to Magnus, section 5, exact: 'Can anything be more learned or more pointed than the style of Tertullian? His Apology and his books Against the Gentiles contain all the wisdom of the world.' (https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf206/npnf206.v.LXX.html)

others_on_him.exact: These things are recorded by Tertullian, a man well versed in the laws of the Romans, and in other respects of high repute, and one of those especially distinguished in Rome.
others_on_him.note: Eusebius read the Apology in a Greek translation. Optional; the first three are stronger.

life_moments.title: A pagan who laughed
life_moments.text: He grew up a pagan in Carthage, well schooled in rhetoric and law. He mocked the Christian faith, as others did. Later he told the pagans that Christians are made, not born.
life_moments.exact: Once these things were with us, too, the theme of ridicule. We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.
life_moments.note: Latin (The Latin Library): 'Haec et nos risimus aliquando. De vestris sumus: Fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani.'

life_moments.title: The Apology
life_moments.text: Christians were being tried and killed for the name alone. He wrote to the Roman governors to defend them. He answered the rumours one by one, and he ended with a warning: killing Christians only makes more of them.
life_moments.exact: The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
life_moments.note: Chapter 1 opens 'Rulers of the Roman Empire'. The New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'addressed to the provincial governors'.

life_moments.title: To the martyrs in prison
life_moments.text: He wrote a short letter to Christians in prison awaiting death. Call it a retreat, he told them, not a prison.
life_moments.exact: Let us drop the name of prison; let us call it a place of retirement.
life_moments.note: Date: the Catholic Encyclopedia puts it in 197 ('The year 197 saw the publication of a short address by Tertullian, To the Martyrs'). Same chapter: 'The leg does not feel the chain when the mind is in the heavens.'

life_moments.title: The New Prophecy
life_moments.text: He came to believe that the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophets of a movement from Phrygia, the New Prophecy. In his own church a woman had visions during Sunday worship, and he trusted them. When Rome turned against the movement, he and his friends left the rest of the Church. He began calling ordinary Christians 'Psychics', the unspiritual.
life_moments.exact: We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete.
life_moments.cite: Against Praxeas, chapter 1; On the Soul, chapter 9; Catholic Encyclopedia
life_moments.note: Catholic Encyclopedia: 'He held the words of Montanus to be really those of the Paraclete'; 'He now terms the Catholics Psychici, as opposed to the spiritual Montanists'; 'when the Montanist prophecies were finally disapproved at Rome, the Church of Carthage excommunicated at least the more violent among their adherents.' The woman: On the Soul 9, exact: 'We have now amongst us a sister whose lot it has been to be favoured with sundry gifts of revelation, which she experiences in the Spirit by ecstatic vision amidst the sacred rites of the Lord's day in the church'. Jerome's version: 'driven by the envy and abuse of the clergy of the Roman church, he lapsed to the doctrine of Montanus' (Illustrious Men 53).
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the Catholic Encyclopedia says the Church of Carthage "excommunicated at least the more violent among their adherents". The saint section had "their fiercest followers"; now "at least the most violent of their followers".

life_moments.title: The soldier's crown
life_moments.text: The army was paid a bonus, and every soldier came up wearing a laurel crown. One carried his in his hand. Asked why, he said, 'I am a Christian.' He gave up his cloak, his boots and his sword and went to prison. Other Christians called him rash. Tertullian wrote a book to defend him.
life_moments.exact: Being urgently asked for his reasons, he answered, I am a Christian.
life_moments.note: Date: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'the donative granted to the army on the accession of Caracalla and Geta in 211'. Same chapter, on the critics' clergy, exact: 'I know, too, their pastors are lions in peace, deer in the fight.'
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: The Chaplet 1 does not say the critics were Christians: "adverse judgments began to be passed upon his conduct—whether on the part of Christians I do not know, for those of the heathen are not different—as if he were headstrong and rash, and too eager to die". The pastors line is about those who "are also purposing the refusal of martyrdom". Page corrected on both points.

life_moments.title: A warning to the governor
life_moments.text: The governor of Africa, Scapula, was persecuting Christians. Tertullian wrote to warn him. Christians pray for their persecutors, he said, and no one should be forced into a religion.
life_moments.exact: It is assuredly no part of religion to compel religion
life_moments.note: Date: Encyclopedia of Religion ('Years later, in 212, he ... addressed to Scapula, proconsul of Africa'). Chapter 2, exact: 'it is a fundamental human right, a privilege of nature, that every man should worship according to his own convictions'. Chapter 1, exact: 'For all love those who love them; it is peculiar to Christians alone to love those that hate them.'
life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: To Scapula 4 says "got rain in that well-known thirst", not "a great thirst". Page now: "in a famous thirst".

life_moments.title: A group of his own
life_moments.text: In time he parted from the Montanists as well, and led his own followers, the Tertullianists. Jerome heard that he lived to a great age. Two centuries later the last of his group came back to the Church in Augustine's day, and handed over their church building.
life_moments.exact: He is said to have lived to a decrepit old age, and to have composed many small works, which are not extant.
life_moments.cite: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53; Augustine, On Heresies 86; Catholic Encyclopedia
life_moments.note: Augustine's Latin: 'Tertullianistae a Tertulliano, cuius multa leguntur opuscula eloquentissime scripta ... Paucissimi enim qui remanserant, in Catholicam transierunt, suamque basilicam, quae nunc etiam notissima est, Catholicae tradiderunt.' The English on tertullian.org beside it is a modern translation (L. G. Muller, 1956, likely still in copyright): paraphrase, do not quote it.

of_him.text: None. No early source tells of a miracle worked by Tertullian, and there is no Life of him. Leave the miracles section out.
of_him.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53 (the only ancient sketch of his life) records none; Vincent's Commonitory 18 records none.

wonders_he_reported.text: OPTIONAL, for the builder to judge: he himself reports wonders of his own day, as things everyone could check. These could sit under 'In his own words' or in the life story, told as he tells them.

items.title: The emperor healed with oil
items.exact: Even Severus himself, the father of Antonine, was graciously mindful of the Christians; for he sought out the Christian Proculus, surnamed Torpacion, the steward of Euhodias, and in gratitude for his having once cured him by anointing, he kept him in his palace till the day of his death.

items.title: Rain for a thirsty army
items.exact: Marcus Aurelius also, in his expedition to Germany, by the prayers his Christian soldiers offered to God, got rain in that well-known thirst.

items.title: Healings and the freed
items.exact: How many men of rank (to say nothing of common people) have been delivered from devils, and healed of diseases!

items.title: A demon at the theatre
items.exact: And in truth I did it most righteously, for I found her in my domain.
items.note: A Christian woman went to the theatre and came home possessed. In the exorcism the demon gave this answer. Tertullian says 'We have the case of the woman ... the Lord Himself is witness'.

wonders_he_reported.note: Tell these as his reports, in his words, never as our claims and never hedged in our voice.

framing.text: These are his own written words, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation (Thelwall and Holmes, 1869 to 1885).

feature.exact: The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
feature.latin: Plures efficimur, quotiens metimur a vobis: semen est sanguis Christianorum.
feature.ctx: The last chapter of the Apology, to the Roman governors. It is the real form of the saying 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church'.
feature.note: The Latin Library marks it section 13 of chapter 50.

lines.exact: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? what between heretics and Christians?
lines.latin: Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis? quid academiae et ecclesiae? quid haereticis et christianis?
lines.ctx: Against mixing philosophy into the faith. He blamed the philosophers for the heresies.
lines.note: Holmes prints a small 'what' before 'between heretics'. It is also his line in 'Where he stood' (learning); use it in one place only, or both deliberately.

lines.exact: We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.
lines.latin: De vestris sumus: Fiunt, non nascuntur Christiani.
lines.ctx: To the pagans. He had been one of them.

lines.exact: O noble testimony of the soul by nature Christian!
lines.ctx: On how people cry out 'God sees' and 'God will repay' without thinking. The source of the famous phrase anima naturaliter Christiana.

lines.exact: We are but of yesterday, and we have filled every place among you
lines.latin: Hesterni sumus, et vestra omnia implevimus
lines.ctx: On how fast the Church had grown. He goes on: cities, islands, the camp, the palace, the senate, 'we have left nothing to you but the temples of your gods'.

lines.exact: Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God.
lines.ctx: On the power of prayer. In the same chapter even the birds 'expand the cross of their wings, and say somewhat to seem like prayer'.

lines.exact: in the Prayer is comprised an epitome of the whole Gospel.
lines.ctx: On the Lord's Prayer. His is the oldest surviving explanation of it.
lines.note: 'Oldest surviving explanation' is NOT sourced here (the claim is common; Origen's On Prayer is later, about 233). Drop it or check it before use.

lines.exact: The leg does not feel the chain when the mind is in the heavens.
lines.ctx: To Christians in prison awaiting death.

lines.exact: If I should offer you a rose, you will not disdain its Maker.
lines.ctx: To Marcion, who despised the Creator. The same chapter praises 'the cells of the bee, the hills of the ant, the webs of the spider'.

lines.exact: Only, I pray that, when you are asking, you be mindful likewise of Tertullian the sinner.
lines.ctx: The last line of his book on baptism, to the newly baptized.
lines.note: A good closing line for the page. Not a prayer to him or by him: he asks for theirs.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'I believe because it is absurd' (Credo quia absurdum).
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not in his writings. He wrote of Christ's death: 'it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd'. He was arguing against Marcion that Christ's flesh was real, and that no one would invent a crucified God. The 'I believe' form came much later. Voltaire gave it the word 'absurd', and first credited it to Augustine.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: And the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd. And He was buried, and rose again; the fact is certain, because it is impossible.
misquoted_or_legend.latin: et mortuus est dei filius: prorsus credibile est, quia ineptum est. et sepultus resurrexit: certum est, quia impossibile.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 5; Peter Harrison, 'I Believe Because it is Absurd: The Enlightenment Invention of Tertullian's Credo', Church History 86 (2017)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Harrison (essay copy on Southern Cross Review): 'The first appearance of the phrase I believe because it is absurd comes subsequently in one of Voltaire's 1767 publications, in which Voltaire attributes to the church father Augustine (rather than to Tertullian), the maxim'. The Latin word is ineptum (foolish, unfitting), not absurdum. The journal article itself was not opened; the essay is by the same author.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.'
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A later smoothing. He wrote 'the blood of Christians is seed'. The words 'martyrs' and 'Church' are not in it.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: the blood of Christians is seed.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'See how these Christians love one another!' as the pagans' praise.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: He does report the pagans saying it. But he says they said it in surprise, because they themselves hated one another.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: See, they say, how they love one another, for themselves are animated by mutual hatred; how they are ready even to die for one another, for they themselves will sooner put to death.
misquoted_or_legend.note: The fathers research called it a pagan 'sneer'. That goes beyond the text: the pagans remark on it, and Tertullian draws the contrast. Say 'in surprise' or just quote it. The ANF editor's own footnote here (CCEL): 'A precious testimony, though the caviller asserts that afterwards the heathen used this expression derisively.'
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Apology 39 frames the remark: "But it is mainly the deeds of a love so noble that lead many to put a brand upon us." The page now quotes "to put a brand upon us" (evidence entry added).

misquoted_or_legend.truth: He is not a saint. The St Tertullian in the Roman Martyrology, on 27 April, is a different man, a bishop of Bologna.
misquoted_or_legend.exact_martyrology: At Bologna, St. Tertullian, bishop and confessor.
misquoted_or_legend.note: Checked in the OCR text (line breaks and double spaces in the scan).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was a priest of Carthage.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Only Jerome says so. In his own books he writes as a layman: 'Are not even we laics priests?' Scholars are divided. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he became a priest; the Encyclopedia of Religion says he was never ordained.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: Are not even we laics priests?
misquoted_or_legend.cite: On Exhortation to Chastity, chapter 7; Jerome, Illustrious Men 53; New Catholic Encyclopedia ('whether he was a priest is still a matter of dispute')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Same chapter: 'But where three are, a church is, albeit they be laics.' The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'He became a priest, no doubt of the Church of Carthage.' Encyclopedia of Religion: 'contrary to Jerome's assumption, he was never ordained a presbyter'. McGiffert's note to Eusebius 2.2: 'That he was a presbyter rests only upon the authority of Jerome'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He was a Roman lawyer, the jurist Tertullianus quoted in Roman law books.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Possible, not proven. Eusebius calls him 'well versed in the laws of the Romans'. Scholars disagree about the jurist.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: Eusebius, Church History, Book 2, chapter 2; Catholic Encyclopedia ('it is doubtful whether he is to be identified with a jurist Tertullian who is cited in the Pandects'); New Catholic Encyclopedia ('It is now generally agreed that he is to be identified with the jurist'); Encyclopedia of Religion ('he probably cannot be identified with the jurist Tertullianus')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Three reference works, three answers. Say 'scholars disagree'.

misquoted_or_legend.truth: He is the first known writer to use it in Latin (trinitas). A Greek writer, Theophilus of Antioch, had already used the Greek word, speaking of 'the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom'.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: types of the Trinity, of God, and His Word, and His wisdom.
misquoted_or_legend.cite: New Catholic Encyclopedia; Theophilus of Antioch, To Autolycus, Book 2, chapter 15 (ANF vol. 2, tr. Marcus Dods)
misquoted_or_legend.note: Theophilus checked in raw anf02.txt (heading 'Chapter XV.--Of the Fourth Day.'). The New Advent URL for Book 2 was not fetched; the CCEL volume was. Theophilus wrote about 180 (not checked here).

misquoted_or_legend.claim: 'Woman, you are the devil's gateway' as his whole view of women.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: He did write it, in a book urging Christian women to dress plainly. The same man wrote the warm picture of marriage to his wife. Quote both.
misquoted_or_legend.exact: You are the devil's gateway: you are the unsealer of that (forbidden) tree: you are the first deserter of the divine law
misquoted_or_legend.cite: On the Apparel of Women, Book 1, chapter 1; To His Wife, Book 2, chapter 8
misquoted_or_legend.note: A hard topic too. Printing it plainly is required by the owner's rules.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He came back to the Church before he died.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: No source says so. The New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'There is no evidence that he returned to the Church before he died.'
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "No source says so" narrowed to "No ancient source says so".

hard_topics.topic: He left the Church for the New Prophecy
hard_topics.holder: Against Praxeas 1 (exact): 'We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete.'
hard_topics.critics: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53 (exact): 'he lapsed to the doctrine of Montanus'. Vincent, Commonitory 18 (exact): 'more eloquent by far than faithful'. Augustine, On Heresies 86 (Latin): 'Non ergo ideo est Tertullianus factus haereticus; sed quia transiens ad Cataphrygas, quos ante destruxerat, coepit etiam secundas nuptias ... tanquam stupra damnare' (He did not become a heretic for that reason [his view that the soul and God are bodies], but because, going over to the Cataphrygians whom he had earlier demolished, he began to condemn second marriages as fornication).
hard_topics.note: The English gloss of Augustine is mine, from the Latin; the tertullian.org English is a modern translation.

hard_topics.holder: On Modesty 21 (exact), which he presents as the Paraclete speaking through the new prophets: 'The Church has the power to forgive sins; but I will not do it, lest they commit others withal.' And On Modesty 1 (exact), mocking a bishop's edict: 'The Pontifex Maximus --that is, the bishop of bishops --issues an edict: "I remit, to such as have discharged (the requirements of) repentance, the sins both of adultery and of fornication."'
hard_topics.critics: New Catholic Encyclopedia: in De pudicitia he 'introduces a distinction between remissible and irremissible sins'; in his earlier On Repentance he had 'placed no restriction of any kind on the Church's power to forgive sins'. Catholic Encyclopedia: the bishop 'is probably Pope Callistus'.
hard_topics.note: The Pontifex Maximus line is in chapter 1 (ccel-modesty-01). Who the bishop was is disputed (Callistus of Rome or Agrippinus of Carthage).

hard_topics.holder: On the Apparel of Women 1.1 (see misquoted). On Baptism 17 (exact): 'For how credible would it seem, that he who has not permitted a woman even to learn with over-boldness, should give a female the power of teaching and of baptizing!'
hard_topics.critics: New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'Sin and death, it is stated, came into the world through a woman; therefore the only proper garb for a woman is the garb of penitence and mourning.' Balance: he trusted a woman prophet in his own congregation (On the Soul 9) and praised 'the most heroic martyr Perpetua' (On the Soul 55).

hard_topics.holder: The Shows 30 (exact): 'How vast a spectacle then bursts upon the eye! What there excites my admiration? what my derision? Which sight gives me joy? which rouses me to exultation?' He means persecuting governors and emperors burning at the Judgment.
hard_topics.critics: New Catholic Encyclopedia: 'in Gibbon's famous indictment he is little better than a sadist' (reporting Gibbon; the article itself calls such estimates exaggerations).
hard_topics.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: The Shows 30: the deified monarchs are "groaning now in the lowest darkness"; it is the persecuting governors who are "in fires more fierce". The page had both "in the flames". Corrected.

hard_topics.critics: The Gelasian Decree, an early list of books to receive and reject, puts 'the works of Tertullian' among the apocrypha, books not received.
hard_topics.note: English by Roger Pearse from von Dobschutz's 1912 Latin edition (tertullian.org). Its date (6th century, credited to Pope Gelasius, prefaced as a Council of Rome under Damasus) is from general knowledge, not checked here: word it as 'a later list'. The New Catholic Encyclopedia mentions 'the condemnation of Tertullian's works by the socalled gelasian decree'.
hard_topics.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: tertullian.org gives no public-domain notice for Roger Pearse's English (checked its translating and about pages), so the page no longer prints "the works of Tertullian" as a quotation. It now says the decree "names his works among the books the Church does not receive".

where_he_stood.text: Sixteen of the quiz's 23 statements. Ten show a line; six are on record but not quoted (anger, tell, nature, calm, rulers, all). Values from site/src/data/which-early-christian.json (people.tertullian.cells). All ten lines are his own words in the ANF translation; each is word for word in the raw volume and on the chapter page named.

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.exact: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church?
rows.note: Irony worth one line on the page: Vincent says he 'comprehended all philosophy', and he let believers learn pagan literature (On Idolatry 10: 'Learning literature is allowable for believers, rather than teaching').

rows.statement: If you had to choose, you'd grow closer to God alone in quiet than among other people.
rows.exact: We are not Indian Brahmins or Gymnosophists, who dwell in woods and exile themselves from ordinary human life.
rows.note: An early (197) view. Later he praised seclusion: To the Martyrs 2 ('The prison does the same service for the Christian which the desert did for the prophet') and On the Pallium 5 ('The better life you would more enjoy in seclusion than in publicity', spoken by the cloak).

rows.statement: Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost.
rows.exact: He who goes before us is not to be lamented, though by all means to be longed for.
rows.note: ANF and New Advent title it 'Of Patience' (the site says 'On Patience'; either is fine, but the chapter page heading reads 'Of Patience' on New Advent and 'On Patience' on CCEL's TOC).

rows.statement: God still speaks to people through dreams.
rows.exact: It was, indeed by an inspiration from God that Nebuchadnezzar dreamt his dreams; and almost the greater part of mankind get their knowledge of God from dreams.
rows.note: Holmes has no comma after 'indeed'; the site copies that exactly.

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.exact: How many men of rank (to say nothing of common people) have been delivered from devils, and healed of diseases!

rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.exact: To know nothing in opposition to the rule (of faith), is to know all things.

rows.statement: In many Bible stories, the deeper meaning matters more than the history.
rows.exact: And, indeed, if all are figures, where will be that of which they are the figures?
rows.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh

rows.statement: If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to.
rows.exact: Parents, wives, children, will have to be left behind, for God's sake. Do you hesitate about arts, and trades, and about professions likewise, for the sake of children and parents?

rows.statement: A church should keep out people who openly live in serious wrongdoing.
rows.exact: Far, far from Christ's betrothed be such a proclamation! She, the true, the modest, the saintly, shall be free from stain even of her ears.
rows.note: Montanist period. The site's note ('He wrote this against a bishop who pardoned adultery after penance') matches chapter 1.

rows.statement: A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience.
rows.exact: The Lord afterward, in disarming Peter, unbelted every soldier.
rows.note: The online CCEL and New Advent copies both read 'unbe**d every soldier' (a corruption). The printed 1869 edition of the same translation reads 'un- belted', and the Latin is 'discinxit' (unbelted). The print also has '[still] the Lord afterward'; the site starts the line at 'The Lord'. The checker matches this line against the archive.org scan text with the hyphen removed. Earlier (Apology 42, 197) he had written 'We sail with you, and fight with you'; his firm view against Christian soldiering is from On Idolatry and The Chaplet 11.

hidden.text: Six scored but not shown: anger (+1, Against Marcion), tell (+1, Apology), nature (-1, Apology), calm (-1, On the Soul), rulers (-1, Apology), all (-2, Apology). Not re-checked: the quiz does not print them.

friends_family_rivals.text: He wrote two books to her, asking her not to remarry after his death, or if she did, to marry only a Christian.
friends_family_rivals.note: Her name is not recorded in the text.

friends_family_rivals.text: The bishop of Carthage a generation later read him every day and called him 'the master', but did not follow him into Montanism.
friends_family_rivals.note: This is the site's existing pair (pairs.cyprian). Cyprian was born after Tertullian's major works; they did not know each other in person, as far as the sources show.

friends_family_rivals.text: He calls her 'the most heroic martyr Perpetua', and cites her vision of Paradise.
friends_family_rivals.note: Some scholars think he edited the account of her martyrdom. Not checked; leave it out.
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: The page had "the vision of Paradise she had on the day she died" in our own voice. On the Soul 55 says she "on the day of her passion saw only her fellow-martyrs there, in the revelation which she received of Paradise"; the Passion itself sets her visions in prison. Page now: "and cites her vision of Paradise".

friends_family_rivals.text: He names Irenaeus among the writers he wants to follow: 'that very exact inquirer into all doctrines'.
friends_family_rivals.exact: Irenæus, that very exact inquirer into all doctrines

friends_family_rivals.text: His great opponent: five books against the man who rejected the Old Testament's God and cut down the Gospels.
friends_family_rivals.note: Marcion died decades before; they never met.

friends_family_rivals.text: A teacher at Rome who made the Father and the Son one person, and turned the bishop of Rome against the New Prophecy. Tertullian: 'he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.'
friends_family_rivals.exact: he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.

friends_family_rivals.text: A painter, probably of Carthage, who taught that matter had always existed. Tertullian wrote a book against him, and mocked him as one who 'mistakes loquacity for eloquence'.
friends_family_rivals.note: Tertullian, Against Hermogenes 1 (exact): 'he despises God’s law in his painting'. 'Probably a Carthaginian, a painter' is the ANF editor's note on the same page, not Tertullian.

friends_family_rivals.text: The governor of Africa to whom he wrote a warning in 212.

friends_family_rivals.who: A bishop he mocked as 'Pontifex Maximus'
friends_family_rivals.text: He issued an edict pardoning adultery after penance. Tertullian answered with On Modesty.
friends_family_rivals.cite: On Modesty, chapter 1; Catholic Encyclopedia ('probably Pope Callistus')

friends_family_rivals.text: Later writers who praised his genius and regretted his Montanism.

how_he_died.text: Nothing is recorded. No source gives the year, the place, the cause or any last words. Jerome only heard that he lived to a very old age. There is no later legend of his death that I found.
how_he_died.exact: He is said to have lived to a decrepit old age
how_he_died.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53; Encyclopedia of Religion ('The exact date of his death is unknown'); New Catholic Encyclopedia ('There is no evidence that he returned to the Church before he died')
how_he_died.note: A short section at most: 'We do not know how he died.' The Latin of Jerome, as quoted by the NCE: 'fertur vixisse usque ad decrepitam aetatem.'

is_he_a_saint.text: No. No church counts him a saint. He left the Church for the New Prophecy and later led his own group. Catholic and Orthodox writers honour his early books and call him a great church writer, but not a saint, and some will not call him a Father.

churches.note: Not in the calendar or the Roman Martyrology. The Gelasian Decree lists his works among books not received.
'Not honoured as a Father of the Church, but recognised as an outstanding church writer' (azbyka.ru).
Not in Common Worship or Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022.
Not in the LCMS or ELCA commemorations.

quotes.exact: In the case of Tertullian we praise his great talent, but we condemn his heresy.
He also was a great trial in the Church.

is_he_a_saint.source: Roman Martyrology (1916); azbyka.ru; Church of England calendar; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LCMS; ELW; New Catholic Encyclopedia; Augustine, On Heresies 86
is_he_a_saint.note: Augustine, On Heresies 86, calls him a heretic ('Tertullianus factus haereticus'), for joining the Cataphrygians (Montanists) and condemning second marriage. New Catholic Encyclopedia's last line: he 'cannot be recommended without reserve to Christian readers or honored with a place among the fathers of the church.' Both on file.

prayer_he_wrote.text: No prayer of his own composition survives that I found. He wrote On Prayer, a commentary on the Lord's Prayer. Two of his books end by asking readers to pray for him or with a blessing that includes him.

items.exact: Only, I pray that, when you are asking, you be mindful likewise of Tertullian the sinner.

To such as read these (exhortations) with good will, to such as prefer Utility to Custom, may peace and grace from our Lord Jesus Christ redound: as likewise to Septimius Tertullianus, whose this tractate is.
items.cite: On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 17

prayer_he_wrote.note: Neither is a prayer to God in form. Leave the 'prayer he wrote' slot out; use the On Baptism line as his closing words on the page.

what_to_read_first.title: The Apology
what_to_read_first.text: His defence of the Christians to the Roman governors, 197. The source of 'the blood of Christians is seed'.
what_to_read_first.check: HTTP 200, title 'CHURCH FATHERS: Apology (Tertullian)', full text on one page (na-apology.txt)

what_to_read_first.title: Of Patience
what_to_read_first.text: Short and personal. It opens with his own impatience.

what_to_read_first.title: To His Wife
what_to_read_first.text: Two short books to his wife, ending with his picture of a Christian marriage.
what_to_read_first.check: HTTP 200, title 'CHURCH FATHERS: To His Wife (Tertullian)'

what_to_read_first.title: The Prescription against Heretics
what_to_read_first.text: Where 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?' comes from, and his case that the Scriptures belong to the Church.
what_to_read_first.check: HTTP 200, title 'CHURCH FATHERS: The Prescription Against Heretics (Tertullian)'

band.artist: André Thevet (book); engraver not named on Commons
band.licence: Public domain. Commons tag {{PD-old-70}} (read from the file page's wikitext).

band.crop: Face at about 50% across, 25% down: suggest --pos-m 55% 20%, --pos-d 55% 18% (check at 320 to 390).

second.title: Tertullien
second.artist: Henri Bonnart (Henri I or II Bonnart), published 'Chez H Bonnart au Coq', Paris
second.date: Undated; the catalogue gives the publisher's range 1600-1750
second.collection: KU Leuven University Libraries, print PA02213
second.alt: A French engraving of Tertullian as an old man with a long white beard and a fur-collared cloak, inside an ornate engraved frame, with a French caption below.
second.caption_text: The caption reads: 'TERTULLIEN Africain natif de Carthage il estoit Payen mais Dieu l'ayant éclairé il fut baptisé peu apres il composa des livres qui contiennent autant de sentences que de mots' (Tertullian, an African born at Carthage. He was a pagan, but God enlightened him and he was baptized soon after. He wrote books with as many maxims as words). That last phrase echoes Vincent of Lerins.
second.note: NOT from the other half of the Church, because none exists: he is not honoured in the East, and I found no icon of him of any date. This is a second Western likeness, deliberately unlike Thevet's (bald and white-bearded against Thevet's turban), which shows the reader these faces are imagined. If the page wants a non-portrait second picture: the 9th-century Codex Agobardinus page (File:Tertullianus Tertullianus Auteur btv1b85722380 193.jpg, PD, but only 455 x 608 on Commons; Gallica's own reuse terms limit commercial use, so avoid fetching the BnF high-res).

personality_test.text: The Christian Personality Test does not name him. 'Tertullian' does not occur in site/src/data/personality.json. The Oak research cites his reading of John the Baptist (Against Marcion 4.18) only as evidence, not as a kindred saint.
personality_test.note: Leave the 'His personality type' field out.

hub_card.text: Hints confirmed: he wrote in Latin at Carthage in the Latin West; his works date from 197 to after 218. 'fathers' is right for the hub's broad group, with the caution in quick_facts.status: Catholic and Orthodox writers withhold the title 'Father' from him. He is not a martyr, monk, desert father or Cappadocian.
hub_card.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('His extant writings range in date from the apologetics of 197 to the attack on a bishop who is probably Pope Callistus (after 218)')
hub_card.note: Same values as design/saints-hub/mockup/src/build.mjs (tertullian: 'fathers', 'pre300', 'west'). Its focus there is '45% 22%'.

site_data_flags.text: people.tertullian.dates 'c. 155 to after 220': the checked sources say about 160 (Catholic Encyclopedia, NCE). Britannica says 155/160. Suggest 'About 160 to after 220' or 'c. 155/160'.

The war line (On Idolatry 19) is right against the printed translation, but the free CCEL and New Advent pages show 'unbe**d'. If the site links the line to CCEL, a reader clicking through sees a garbled word. Consider linking the archive.org scan or adding a note.
The README's status line 'Church Father. Not counted a saint.' conflicts with two sources that deny him the title Father (NCE; azbyka.ru). See quick_facts.status.
The fathers research's 'misattributed' note calls the Apology 39 'see how they love one another' line a 'sneer'. The text does not say sneer. Softened here.
The fathers research's 'Vain and silly topics are met with special fitness' is New Advent's wording; CCEL (the ANF as printed on CCEL) has 'especial'.

The research's 'On Flight in Persecution, section 14' for 'He who fears to suffer, cannot belong to Him who suffered' is right. The ANF prints De Fuga without chapter numbers, but the Latin (The Latin Library) has the line in chapter 14, section 3: 'Non potest, qui pati timet, ei esse, qui passus est'. The English is word for word on CCEL's single page (ccel-flight.txt; url https://ccel.org/ccel/schaff/anf04/anf04.iii.x.i.html).
site_data_flags.exact: He who fears to suffer, cannot belong to Him who suffered.

could_not_verify: Britannica's page (403 to curl and WebFetch). Its dates 'born c. 155/160, Carthage; died after 220, Carthage' were read only in a search-engine summary. The place of death rests on Britannica alone.
Merriam-Webster and Collins's own pages (403). Pronunciation is taken from Dictionary.com, which prints both Random House and Collins.
That no ancient or medieval likeness of him exists. It is an absence: nothing older than the 1584 engravings appears on Commons except manuscripts of his text.
The date of the Gelasian Decree and of Vincent's Commonitory (about 434); both from general knowledge, not re-read.
That On Prayer is the oldest surviving commentary on the Lord's Prayer (common claim; not sourced here).
Whether he edited the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (some scholars think so; not checked, not used).
The 2004 Roman Martyrology (only the 1916 English edition was checked for his absence and for St Tertullian of Bologna).
The Great Synaxaristes and GOARCH for his absence (the Orthodox answer rests on azbyka.ru and OCA search; he is not expected there).
Theophilus of Antioch's date (about 180) and the New Advent URL for To Autolycus Book 2; the line itself is checked in CCEL's anf02.txt.
Peter Harrison's journal article itself (Church History 86, 2017); the essay by him on Southern Cross Review was read.
Pamelius 1584 woodcuts on Commons (downloads failed; not inspected).
